glance.label: Main Idea
glance.html: Proverbs 24 sets a house built by wisdom beside a field ruined by neglect, and between them calls the son to rescue the perishing, rise again after trouble, refuse gloating and revenge, and fear the LORD.

glance.label: Setting
glance.html: Verses 1–22 finish “the words of the wise” begun at 22:17, still addressed to “My son” (24:13, 21). A short appendix, “These things also belong to the wise” (24:23), ends at the lazy man’s field.

glance.label: Key Verse
glance.html: “Through wisdom a house is built, And by understanding it is established; By knowledge the rooms are filled With all precious and pleasant riches.” (Proverbs 24:3–4)

cards.title: The Heart of the Chapter
cards.html:
Proverbs 24 opens with a house and closes with a field. “Through wisdom a house is built” (24:3), and knowledge fills its rooms “With all precious and pleasant riches” (24:4). At the other end lies a vineyard where “Its stone wall was broken down” (24:31). No enemy did that damage; a little folding of the hands did. Between them stands the wisdom that builds: skill for living life God’s way, a strength that holds in adversity and moves to “Deliver those who are drawn toward death” (24:10–11).

The chapter keeps the son’s eyes on God. Whoever pleads, “Surely we did not know this,” faces “He who weighs the hearts” (24:12), who will “render to each man according to his deeds.” So the son must not gloat over a fallen enemy, “Lest the LORD see it” (24:18), or say, “I will render to the man according to his work” (24:29), because repaying belongs to God. The righteous may fall seven times and rise again (24:16), and the fear of the LORD, a right view of God, frees him from envying the wicked, whose lamp will be put out (24:19–21).

The appendix applies this wisdom to the courtroom and the field, ending with a wise man who learns from another’s ruin: “I considered it well” (24:32).

cards.title: Chapter Sections
cards.html:
Proverbs 24:1–6 — Wisdom Builds a House

The son is told not to envy evil men, whose hearts and lips are busy with violence and trouble, because wisdom builds a house, understanding makes it secure, and knowledge fills its rooms with what is precious and pleasant. The same wisdom is strength, for a man wages war by wise counsel and finds safety among many counselors rather than going it alone.

Proverbs 24:7–12 — Strength in Adversity and Rescue for the Perishing

Three short sayings name the fool who has nothing to say at the city gate, the plotter who earns the name of schemer, and the scoffer whom people find detestable. Then the son is tested: strength that faints in adversity is small, and he must rescue those being dragged toward death, because the God who weighs the hearts sees through the excuse “Surely we did not know this” (24:12) and will repay each man for his deeds.

Proverbs 24:13–16 — Sweet Wisdom and the Righteous Who Rise Again

Honey is good and sweet to the taste, and the knowledge of wisdom is just as good to the soul, bringing a future and a hope that will not be cut off (compare 23:18). The wicked man is warned to his face not to raid the home of the righteous, for the righteous may be knocked down by trouble seven times and still rise, while the wicked are brought down by calamity.

Proverbs 24:17–22 — Do Not Gloat or Fret; Fear the LORD

The son must not be glad when his enemy stumbles, because gloating displeases the LORD, and he must not fret over or envy evildoers, whose lamp will be put out. He is to fear the LORD and the king and keep away from “those given to change” (24:21), most likely people bent on overturning order, whose ruin can come without warning.

Proverbs 24:23–29 — Further Sayings of the Wise

A new heading adds sayings that also belong to the wise: partiality in judgment is not good, and whoever calls the wicked righteous is cursed by the people and abhorred by nations, while honest rebuke brings blessing and a right answer is like a kiss on the lips. The son is to prepare his fields before he builds his house, to refuse to testify against a neighbor without cause, and to leave repayment to God instead of vowing to treat others as they treated him.

Proverbs 24:30–34 — The Field of the Lazy Man

The wise man walks past a lazy man’s field and vineyard, sees thorns, nettles, and a broken stone wall, and takes the lesson to heart. The ruin came through small, repeated rests, and want arrives as suddenly as an armed man; the warning concerns willful neglect, not need that comes from inability or genuine hardship.

cards.title: Why This Chapter Matters
cards.html:
Proverbs 24 will not let wisdom stay at home. The chapter that praises a well-furnished house also sends the son to rescue those stumbling to the slaughter (24:11) and removes the excuse of not knowing, because God weighs the heart behind it. Strength that faints when rescue grows costly is small (24:10).

The chapter also guards the heart toward enemies. Envy, fretting, gloating, and revenge all let the wicked set the terms of a life, and Proverbs 24 forbids each (24:1, 17–19, 29). Jesus carries this further in commanding love for enemies (Matthew 5:44), and Paul writes, “Repay no one evil for evil” (Romans 12:17). The neglected field adds a quieter warning: ruin seldom comes in a day, though Proverbs never confuses laziness with genuine inability or hardship.

cards.title: Key Themes to Watch For
cards.html:
Building and ruin. Wisdom builds and furnishes a house, and work is put in order before the house is built, while neglect leaves a wall broken down (24:3–4, 27, 30–31).

Nothing to envy in the wicked. Evil men plot violence and have no future, so neither their company nor their success is worth wanting (24:1–2, 19–20).

Courage to rescue. Adversity tests a person’s strength, and the God who weighs the hearts does not accept ignorance as a reason for standing by (24:10–12).

Rising again. Trouble may knock the righteous down again and again without finishing him, while calamity brings the wicked down (24:15–16).

Justice without favoritism or revenge. The wise judge fairly, rebuke the wicked honestly, refuse false witness, and do not pay back what was done to them (24:23–26, 28–29).

cards.title: Key Words & Concepts
cards.html:
Schemer (24:8). A person known for plotting harm. What a man keeps planning in secret eventually becomes the name others give him.

An abomination to men (24:9). Proverbs often names what is “an abomination to the LORD” (11:1; 15:8). Here it is people who find the scoffer detestable, because his mockery of correction makes him repugnant even to others.

He who weighs the hearts (24:12). A picture of God measuring motives as if on a scale (compare 21:2). He knows whether “we did not know” is true, and He will repay accordingly.

Seven times (24:16). A way of saying again and again. In context the falls are troubles the wicked bring on the righteous, and the saying offers no excuse for repeated sin.

The fear of the LORD (24:21). A right view of God: terror for those who defy Him, and awe for all at His glory, majesty, and holiness, for He is unlike any other. It comes before respect for the king and never requires obeying a ruler who commands what God forbids (Acts 5:29).

The lazy man (24:30). The NKJV’s word here; it uses “sluggard” only in 6:6 and 6:9. He is also called “the man devoid of understanding” (24:30), because his trouble is a lack of sense and self-discipline, not a lack of ability.

1.brief: Do not envy evil men or wish to be in their company. The son is warned against the quiet pull of admiring the wicked and wanting to belong among them.
1.explain:
“Do not be envious of evil men,”

The words of the wise return to a danger already named in 23:17. Evil men often seem to do well. They take what they want, answer to no one, and appear free of the restraints the son lives under. Envy is the quiet resentment and longing that such success can stir. The command is to refuse it. Envy of the wicked is dangerous because it slowly changes what a person admires.

“Nor desire to be with them;”

Envy easily turns into a wish to belong. The son is warned not to “desire to be with them,” not to want a place in their company. Proverbs began with the same warning, when sinners invited the son to “Come with us” and share their loot (1:11). What a person admires he soon wants to join, and what he joins he soon becomes. The next verse shows what the son would be joining.

2.brief: Their hearts plot violence, and their lips talk about making trouble. Seen for what they really are, evil men offer nothing worth envying, since everything inside and everything they say aims at harm.
2.explain:
“For their heart devises violence,”

The reason not to envy evil men is what they are like inside. Their “heart devises violence.” Their inner life is busy planning harm to others. What looks like freedom or success from the outside is, at its core, a mind given over to violence.

“And their lips talk of troublemaking.”

Their speech matches their hearts. Their “lips talk of troublemaking,” the schemes and mischief they plan for others. Heart and mouth together are aimed at harm. Seen for what they really are, evil men offer nothing worth envying. The son who looks past their apparent success to the heart and the lips will see that their company is a place of trouble, not freedom. The contrast with the next verse is deliberate: the wicked plan to tear down, while wisdom builds.

3.brief: A house is built by wisdom and made secure by understanding. Over against the violence of the wicked, wisdom is pictured as a builder, and the houses of a life, such as a marriage, a family, or a livelihood, show the mark of the wisdom or folly behind them.
3.explain:
“Through wisdom a house is built,”

Over against the violence of the wicked, wisdom is pictured as a builder. A “house” is first a dwelling, and in Proverbs it also means a household: the family, the life, and the livelihood a person builds. Wisdom, skill for living God’s way, is what builds it. Proverbs uses the same picture of Wisdom herself, who “has built her house” (9:1), and of the wise woman who “builds her house” (14:1).

“And by understanding it is established;”

Building is not enough; the house must stand. “Understanding” makes it “established,” firm and secure, able to last. The houses of a life, such as a marriage, a family, a business, or a ministry, show the mark of the wisdom or folly behind them. What has been built reveals the builder. This is not meant to condemn those whose homes have suffered loss through no fault of their own. It calls for honest examination of what one is building and with what tools.
3.notes: The three Hebrew words of 24:3–4 for wisdom, understanding, and knowledge are the same three used of the LORD’s own work in creation, and the verb for “established” in 24:3 is the one used there of the heavens: “The LORD by wisdom founded the earth; By understanding He established the heavens; By His knowledge the depths were broken up” (3:19–20). The builder of a household works with the same qualities by which God made the world.

4.brief: Through knowledge the rooms are filled with every kind of precious and pleasant treasure. Wisdom does more than raise the walls; it furnishes the house with what makes it rich and good to live in.
4.explain:
“By knowledge the rooms are filled”

Wisdom does more than raise walls. “By knowledge the rooms are filled.” Knowledge here is practical understanding of how to live, manage, and provide. It furnishes the house so that it becomes a place worth living in.

“With all precious and pleasant riches.”

The rooms are filled “With all precious and pleasant riches.” The riches are both valuable and delightful. In a household, they may include material provision, and they also include the things that make a home rich in the fuller sense: peace, love, good order, and joy. Like other sayings about reward, this describes what wisdom tends to produce under God’s blessing, not a promise of wealth. The picture stands in sharp contrast to the neglected field at the end of the chapter, described in 24:30–31, where a stone wall that was once built has been left to fall and weeds have overrun the ground. Wisdom builds a house and keeps it in good order; neglect lets even what was built fall into ruin.

5.brief: A wise man is strong, and a man of knowledge grows in strength. Wisdom is a kind of power, often greater than physical might.
5.explain:
“A wise man is strong,”

Wisdom is a form of strength. “A wise man is strong.” Strength in the ancient world usually meant physical might or military power, but the wise man has a strength of his own: the ability to see clearly, plan well, and act effectively.

“Yes, a man of knowledge increases strength;”

The second line goes further. “A man of knowledge increases strength.” Knowledge does not merely give a fixed amount of power; it multiplies it. A strong man without wisdom may waste his strength, while a wise man uses whatever strength he has to the best effect. The saying prepares for the next verse, where wisdom proves itself on the battlefield. Ecclesiastes says the same: “Wisdom is better than strength” (Ecclesiastes 9:16).
5.notes: The Hebrew wording is more vivid than the English. The KJV margin notes that the first line says literally that a wise man is in strength, and that the second says a man of knowledge “strengtheneth might,” that is, he makes his strength greater. The literal wording supports the point of the verse: knowledge does not merely possess strength but builds it up.

6.brief: Wise guidance lets a person wage his battles, and safety is found where there are many counselors. Strength comes from seeking and heeding sound advice, not from going it alone (compare 11:14).
6.explain:
“For by wise counsel you will wage your own war,”

The reason wisdom is strength is that wars are won by “wise counsel,” sound guidance and good strategy. A king who plans his campaign carefully, using wise advice, can “wage your own war” successfully. The same is true of any struggle a person faces. Proverbs has already said, “By wise counsel wage war” (20:18).

“And in a multitude of counselors there is safety.”

Wise counsel usually comes from more than one person. “In a multitude of counselors there is safety.” A leader who listens to many wise advisers sees more clearly, catches mistakes, and avoids disaster. This repeats 11:14 almost exactly. Strength comes from seeking and heeding good advice, not from relying only on oneself. Pride that refuses counsel is weakness, however strong it looks.
6.notes: The second line repeats the second line of 11:14, “But in the multitude of counselors there is safety” (11:14).

7.brief: Wisdom is out of the fool’s reach, so he has nothing to say at the city gate where matters are decided. When serious affairs are discussed, the fool has no useful word to offer.
7.explain:
“Wisdom is too lofty for a fool;”

To the fool, wisdom is “too lofty,” high above him and out of reach. The problem is not that wisdom is hidden. Proverbs shows Wisdom calling openly in the streets in 1:20–21. The fool cannot reach wisdom because he despises it and will not stoop to learn.

“He does not open his mouth in the gate.”

The “gate” of the city was where the elders met, cases were judged, and public matters were decided. When serious affairs are discussed there, the fool “does not open his mouth.” He has nothing useful to say. Elsewhere Proverbs shows the fool talking constantly, but in the place where wisdom counts, he has no word to offer. His silence at the gate exposes his emptiness.

8.brief: Whoever plans to do evil will come to be known as a schemer. A person’s settled intentions eventually become his reputation and his name.
8.explain:
“He who plots to do evil”

This person “plots to do evil.” He is not someone who stumbles into wrong on impulse. He plans it, turns it over in his mind, and designs his schemes.

“Will be called a schemer.”

In time he “Will be called a schemer.” In Hebrew he is literally called a master of schemes, and that is how others know him. A person’s settled intentions become his reputation. What he plans in secret eventually becomes his public name. Just as the proud man earns the name “Scoffer” (21:24), the plotter earns the name schemer. The verse warns that our inner plans do not stay hidden; they become who we are.

9.brief: Plotting folly is sin, and people find the scoffer detestable. Wrongdoing begins in what is devised before it is done, and the mocker’s contempt makes him repugnant to others.
9.explain:
“The devising of foolishness is sin,”

The verse goes to the root. Sin is not only in the doing; it is in “The devising of foolishness.” Planning folly, scheming what is wrong, is already sin before any act follows. Proverbs consistently traces conduct back to the heart, and here the plans of the heart are themselves judged.

“And the scoffer is an abomination to men.”

The second line names the scoffer, the proud mocker who will not be corrected. He is “an abomination to men.” Proverbs often speaks of what is an abomination to the LORD, but here it is people who find the scoffer detestable. His constant contempt, mockery, and refusal to be taught make him repugnant even to others. The scoffer does not only offend God; he makes himself unbearable to everyone around him.

10.brief: If you lose heart when trouble comes, your strength is small. Adversity reveals how much strength a person really has, and the saying prepares for the hard demand that follows.
10.explain:
“If you faint in the day of adversity,”

The “day of adversity” is a time of trouble or distress. To “faint” is to lose heart, give up, or collapse under the pressure. The verse imagines the son facing a hard time and failing to hold up.

“Your strength is small.”

The conclusion is blunt: “Your strength is small.” Adversity reveals how much strength a person really has. Strength that holds only when things are easy is not much strength. The saying prepares for the hard command in 24:11–12, where the son must rescue those in danger even when it is costly. Real strength is shown in persevering through difficulty, and for the believer that strength comes from God, who gives power to the weak.
10.notes: In Hebrew, “adversity” (tsarah) and “small” (tsar) sound alike, and both come from words for narrowness: the day of adversity is a day of tight straits, and strength that gives way in it is narrow strength. The play on words ties the two lines together and sharpens the rebuke, because the narrow place exposes how narrow a person’s strength really is.

11.brief: Rescue those who are being dragged toward death, and hold back those staggering toward slaughter. Wisdom does not stand by while others are led to destruction, even when stepping in is costly.
11.explain:
“Deliver those who are drawn toward death,”

The command is to rescue. Some people are being “drawn toward death,” dragged or led toward destruction. The verse does not say who they are or why, and the language could include people unjustly condemned, those led away to be killed, and anyone heading toward ruin. The son is told to “Deliver” them, stepping in to save them.

“And hold back those stumbling to the slaughter.”

The second line repeats the command. The son must “hold back,” restrain and protect, “those stumbling to the slaughter.” They are staggering toward a violent death and cannot save themselves. Wisdom does not stand by while others are led to destruction, even when stepping in is costly. This follows directly from 24:10: rescue takes strength, and the person who faints in adversity will not do it. The verse applies broadly to injustice and danger wherever they are found, and it calls for action, not just sympathy.

12.brief: If you say, “Surely we did not know this,” God who weighs the heart sees through the excuse. He guards your life, He knows the truth, and He will repay each person according to what he has done, so pleading ignorance does not cover indifference.
12.explain:
“If you say, ‘Surely we did not know this,’”

The son might try to excuse himself: “Surely we did not know this.” It is the oldest excuse for doing nothing. We did not know, we did not see, it was not our business. The verse anticipates this plea and answers it.

“Does not He who weighs the hearts consider it?”

God “weighs the hearts” (21:2). He knows whether the excuse is true. He sees whether the son truly did not know or chose not to know. Ignorance that is willful is not innocence.

“He who keeps your soul, does He not know it?”

The same God “keeps your soul,” guarding and preserving your life. The One who watches over the son also watches the son’s response to others in danger. He knows everything.

“And will He not render to each man according to his deeds?”

Finally, God will “render to each man according to his deeds.” He will repay. Indifference to those being dragged toward death is not neutral. It will be judged. Pleading ignorance does not cover indifference before God.
12.notes: Paul states the same principle in Romans 2:6, “who will render to each one according to his deeds” (Romans 2:6), and Psalm 62:12 says the same of God in different Hebrew words.

13.brief: My son, eat honey because it is good, and the honeycomb because it is sweet to the taste. The father begins with an everyday pleasure to set up a comparison.
13.explain:
“My son, eat honey because it is good,”

The father turns to an everyday pleasure. Honey was prized for its sweetness, and the father tells the son to “eat honey because it is good.” There is nothing wrong with enjoying it. This sets up a comparison.

“And the honeycomb which is sweet to your taste;”

The honeycomb, honey straight from the comb, was especially prized. It is “sweet to your taste.” The father draws attention to the pleasure of the senses so that the next verse can point beyond it. Just as honey delights the tongue, something else will delight the soul. Proverbs does not treat pleasure as suspect in itself; it uses an ordinary good to point toward a greater one.

14.brief: Wisdom is just as sweet and good for the soul, and whoever finds it has a future and a hope that will not be cut off. The pleasure of honey points to a deeper sweetness that also lasts (compare 23:18).
14.explain:
“So shall the knowledge of wisdom be to your soul;”

Here is the point of the comparison. As honey is sweet and good to the body, “So shall the knowledge of wisdom be to your soul.” Wisdom is not only useful; it is sweet. The person who comes to know it finds it delightful, nourishing, and satisfying. The psalmist said the same of God’s word: “Sweeter also than honey and the honeycomb” (Psalm 19:10).

“If you have found it, there is a prospect,”

Wisdom also has a future. “If you have found it, there is a prospect,” a hopeful outcome ahead. Honey’s sweetness passes quickly, but wisdom’s good lasts.

“And your hope will not be cut off.”

The promise echoes 23:18 almost word for word. The person who finds wisdom has a hope that “will not be cut off.” It will not be disappointed or destroyed. The wicked have no future, as 24:20 will say, but the one who finds wisdom has a lasting hope under God.
14.notes: In Hebrew, “prospect” is the same word rendered “hereafter” in 23:18, a word for an end or future outcome, and the final line of the two verses is identical in the NKJV.

15.brief: The wicked man is addressed directly and told not to lie in ambush against the home of the righteous or raid his resting place. The warning is aimed at the one who plans to ruin the godly.
15.explain:
“Do not lie in wait, O wicked man, against the dwelling of the righteous;”

The address changes. The wicked man himself is spoken to directly: “O wicked man.” He is told not to “lie in wait” against the home of the righteous, hiding in ambush to attack or rob. The warning anticipates his plans.

“Do not plunder his resting place;”

The second line repeats the warning. The wicked man must not “plunder his resting place,” the home where the righteous man lives and rests. The command carries the weight of a verdict: such plans will not have the last word. Throughout Proverbs the wicked plot against the righteous, and here the teacher turns and speaks to the plotter himself. The next verse gives the reason his plans cannot finally succeed.

16.brief: Though a righteous man falls seven times, he rises again, but the wicked are brought down by calamity. The falls here are troubles and setbacks the righteous suffer, yet under God’s care they are not finally overthrown; the saying gives no excuse for repeated sin.
16.explain:
“For a righteous man may fall seven times”

The reason the wicked man’s plans cannot finally succeed is that the righteous cannot be finally defeated. He “may fall seven times.” Seven times means again and again, as often as trouble comes. In context, the falls are the troubles and setbacks the wicked bring on him, attacks and losses that knock him down.

“And rise again,”

Yet he will “rise again.” He is not finally overthrown. The righteous man gets back up, not by his own strength alone, but because God upholds him. Micah expressed the same confidence: “When I fall, I will arise” (Micah 7:8). The saying does not promise that every loss will be quickly restored. The righteous may suffer real and lasting loss in this life, and the rising may be slow or may come only at the end. What the verse promises is that the one God upholds is not finally overthrown. The verse is not an excuse for repeated sin. It is a promise of resilience under God’s care, and where it is applied to failure, repentance remains central.

“But the wicked shall fall by calamity.”

The wicked man, by contrast, “shall fall by calamity.” His fall carries no promise of rising. The righteous may be knocked down many times and still be upheld, but the wicked may fall once and be finished. This is why the wicked man is warned in 24:15: his attacks on the righteous cannot finally prevail, while his own end is ruin.
16.notes: Psalm 37 uses a similar picture of the righteous: “Though he fall, he shall not be utterly cast down; For the LORD upholds him with His hand” (Psalm 37:24).

17.brief: Do not celebrate when your enemy falls, and do not let your heart be glad when he stumbles. Gloating over another’s ruin is forbidden even when that person has been an enemy.
17.explain:
“Do not rejoice when your enemy falls,”

The command is surprising in a world where victory over an enemy was celebrated. The son must “not rejoice when your enemy falls.” Even when someone has truly been an enemy, his downfall is not an occasion for glee. Job counted it among the sins he had not committed: “If I have rejoiced at the destruction of him who hated me” (Job 31:29).

“And do not let your heart be glad when he stumbles;”

The second line goes deeper. It is not enough to avoid public celebration; the son must not even “let your heart be glad.” Gloating can happen silently, inside. The command reaches to the private satisfaction a person might feel when someone who hurt him suffers. God cares about the heart’s response to an enemy’s trouble, not only about outward behavior. Proverbs elsewhere calls for kindness to an enemy in need, as in 25:21, and Jesus carried this teaching further when He said, “love your enemies” (Matthew 5:44).

18.brief: The LORD may see it, be displeased, and turn His anger away from the enemy. The point is the condition of the gloater’s own heart, which offends God, not a technique for making an enemy suffer more.
18.explain:
“Lest the LORD see it, and it displease Him,”

The reason is that the LORD sees the gloating heart, “and it displease Him.” Gloating over another’s ruin is itself a sin. It reveals pride, cruelty, and a heart that has forgotten its own need of mercy. The LORD who weighs the hearts, as 24:12 has just said, sees the satisfaction the son takes in his enemy’s fall.

“And He turn away His wrath from him.”

The result is that God might “turn away His wrath from him,” that is, from the enemy. The point is not a technique for making an enemy suffer more by hiding one’s joy. The point is that gloating offends God so much that He may turn His attention from the enemy’s guilt to the gloater’s. Judgment belongs to God, and the person who celebrates another’s downfall has stepped into a place that is not his. The verse guards the son’s own heart.

19.brief: Do not fret over evildoers or envy the wicked. The son is told again not to let the apparent success of the wicked stir him to worry or jealousy (compare verse 1).
19.explain:
“Do not fret because of evildoers,”

The son is warned again about his response to the wicked. To “fret” is to become agitated, anxious, or angry, burning inside over the apparent success of “evildoers.” The sight of wicked people prospering can stir up resentment and worry in the righteous.

“Nor be envious of the wicked;”

The second line returns to envy, the danger named in 24:1. The son must not be “envious of the wicked,” wishing he had what they have or could live as they live. Fretting and envy both let the wicked set the terms of the son’s inner life. The next verse gives the reason he does not need either.
19.notes: The first line is identical in the NKJV to the opening of Psalm 37, “Do not fret because of evildoers” (Psalm 37:1), a psalm that treats the same temptation at length.

20.brief: The evil man has no future, and the lamp of the wicked will be snuffed out. Whatever the wicked seem to have now, their life and prosperity will not last, so there is nothing to envy.
20.explain:
“For there will be no prospect for the evil man;”

The reason not to envy the wicked is that they have no future. “There will be no prospect for the evil man.” In Hebrew, “prospect” is the same word used in 24:14 for the hope of the one who finds wisdom. The wise have a future that will not be cut off. The evil man has none. Whatever he seems to enjoy now will not last.

“The lamp of the wicked will be put out.”

The second line uses a familiar image. A “lamp” burning in a house was a sign of life and of a household that continued. For “The lamp of the wicked” to be “put out” is for his life and his house to come to an end, plunged into darkness. Proverbs used the same words in 13:9. The prosperity of the wicked is like a lamp that seems bright for a while but will be snuffed out. There is nothing to envy in that.
20.notes: The second line repeats the second line of 13:9 word for word in the NKJV: “But the lamp of the wicked will be put out” (13:9).

21.brief: My son, fear the LORD and the king, and do not join with those who are given to change. Reverence for God comes first and respect for rightful authority follows; “those given to change” most likely describes people bent on overturning order, and the son is to keep away from them.
21.explain:
“My son, fear the LORD and the king;”

The son is called to “fear the LORD,” to hold a right view of God that produces awe, reverence, and obedience. That comes first. The “king” follows. Respect for rightful authority is part of wisdom, because God has ordained government for the good of society. Yet the order of the words matters. The LORD comes before the king, and loyalty to God always takes precedence. Peter puts the two in the same order: “Fear God. Honor the king” (1 Peter 2:17). When a ruler commands what God forbids, the answer is that of the apostles: “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29).

“Do not associate with those given to change;”

The son must not join “those given to change.” The phrase most likely describes people bent on overturning order, rebels and agitators who stir up revolt against rightful authority. The son is to keep away from them. The warning is not against all change or reform but against reckless rebellion that throws off both the fear of God and respect for legitimate authority.
21.notes: The meaning of “those given to change” is debated. The Hebrew is a form of the verb to change, which the KJV margin renders literally “changers.” Earlier editions of the NIV and the NLT interpret it as rebels, and the ESV renders it as those who do otherwise, that is, those who do not fear the LORD and the king.

22.brief: Calamity can rise against such people suddenly, and who knows the ruin the LORD and the king can bring? The warning is against joining reckless revolt; it does not place God behind every ruler or require obedience when rulers command what God forbids (Acts 5:29).
22.explain:
“For their calamity will rise suddenly,”

The reason for the warning is that disaster comes on rebels without warning. “Their calamity will rise suddenly.” Those who join reckless revolt may expect success, but ruin can fall on them all at once.

“And who knows the ruin those two can bring?”

“Those two” are the LORD and the king named in 24:21. Who can measure the ruin they can bring on those who defy them? The LORD judges those who rebel against Him, and rulers punish those who rise against them. The warning is against joining rebellion that despises God and rightful authority. It does not place God behind every ruler’s decision, and it does not require obedience when rulers command what God forbids. It counsels the son to keep away from people whose path leads to sudden ruin.
22.notes: With this verse the collection introduced at 22:17 ends. A second, shorter collection of sayings of the wise begins at 24:23.

23.brief: A new heading announces further sayings that also belong to the wise, beginning with the warning that showing partiality in judgment is not good. Justice must be fair, never bent by favoritism toward one side.
23.explain:
“These things also belong to the wise:”

A new heading announces further sayings that “also belong to the wise.” It marks a short appendix to the collection that began at 22:17 and shows that these sayings, too, come from wise teachers. The words of the wise continue, applied now to the courtroom and the field.

“It is not good to show partiality in judgment.”

The first saying addresses the courts. To “show partiality in judgment” is in Hebrew literally to recognize faces, favoring someone because of who he is, whether rich, powerful, a friend, or a relative. Justice must be fair to all. The law of Moses said the same: “You shall not show partiality in judgment; you shall hear the small as well as the great” (Deuteronomy 1:17). Partiality corrupts justice and harms those who have no one to speak for them.

24.brief: The person who tells the guilty, “You are righteous,” will be cursed by people and hated by nations. Calling evil good provokes the outrage of everyone who longs for justice.
24.explain:
“He who says to the wicked, ‘You are righteous,’”

This is the corrupt judge or witness who tells the guilty, “You are righteous.” He declares the guilty innocent, perhaps for a bribe, perhaps out of fear or favoritism. He calls evil good. Proverbs says elsewhere, “He who justifies the wicked, and he who condemns the just, Both of them alike are an abomination to the LORD” (17:15).

“Him the people will curse;”

The result is that “the people will curse” him. Ordinary people know when justice has been perverted. They feel it, and they curse the one who did it.

“Nations will abhor him.”

The second line widens the reaction. “Nations will abhor him.” Calling evil good provokes the outrage of everyone who longs for justice. Even people far from Israel recognize that a judge who acquits the guilty is a disgrace. The verse shows that the sense of justice God has placed in human beings rises up against such corruption.

25.brief: Those who rebuke the wicked will find delight, and a rich blessing will come on them. Honest confrontation of wrongdoing is commended and rewarded, in contrast to the flattery of verse 24.
25.explain:
“But those who rebuke the wicked will have delight,”

The contrast is the person who will not flatter the guilty but rebukes them. Those who “rebuke the wicked” tell the truth about wrongdoing, whether in court or in daily life. They “will have delight.” Honest confrontation of wrong, though it may be hard at the moment, brings good results and favor.

“And a good blessing will come upon them.”

Further, “a good blessing will come upon them.” The verse does not say who gives the blessing. A natural counterpart to the people’s curse in 24:24 is their blessing on the one who tells the truth, though the verse does not limit the blessing to them. Honesty and courage in the face of wrongdoing are commended and rewarded. The saying encourages the son to be the kind of person who speaks the truth about wrong rather than covering it up.

26.brief: Giving an honest answer is like a kiss on the lips. A straight, truthful reply is a mark of real friendship and affection, however much flattery may seem kinder.
26.explain:
“He who gives a right answer kisses the lips.”

The single line is a vivid image. To give “a right answer” is to give an honest, straightforward reply. Such a person “kisses the lips.” The proverb compares an honest answer to an affectionate kiss. An honest answer is an act of love. Flattery may seem kinder in the moment, but truth told straight is the mark of a real friend. The saying fits the surrounding verses about justice. In court and in life, the honest word is what binds people together in trust. Partiality, false acquittal, and false witness all corrupt the truth, and this saying sets the plain, right answer against them.
26.notes: The KJV margin gives the Hebrew wording of the second half literally as one “that answereth” right words, that is, one who replies with straight, honest words. The Hebrew word for “right” here means straight or straightforward.

27.brief: Get your work outside in order and prepare your fields, and after that build your house. Wisdom puts first things first, securing a livelihood before taking on the costs of establishing a household.
27.explain:
“Prepare your outside work,”

The saying turns to practical order. The son must “Prepare your outside work,” getting the fields ready, plowing and planting, securing a source of income. In an agricultural society, the fields were the livelihood.

“Make it fit for yourself in the field;”

He must make the field fit, ready to produce. This takes planning and effort. Only when the livelihood is secure is the time right for the next step.

“And afterward build your house.”

Then, “afterward build your house.” A house here may be the building itself, and it may also mean establishing a household by marrying and raising a family. Either way, wisdom puts first things first. Securing a livelihood comes before taking on the costs of building or establishing a home. The person who reverses the order may end with a house he cannot support. The saying is practical wisdom about planning and priorities.

28.brief: Do not testify against your neighbor without cause, and do not deceive with your lips. False or needless testimony betrays a neighbor and corrupts justice.
28.explain:
“Do not be a witness against your neighbor without cause,”

The son must not testify against his neighbor “without cause.” This may mean false testimony, or it may mean needless testimony, bringing an accusation that has no basis or serves no just purpose. Either way, it betrays a neighbor and corrupts justice. The commandment says, “You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor” (Exodus 20:16).

“For would you deceive with your lips?”

The question makes the son face what he would be doing. “Would you deceive with your lips?” To testify without cause is to use one’s mouth to deceive. The question appeals to the son’s conscience. A wise person does not want his lips to be instruments of deceit.

29.brief: The son must not say that he will do to another just as was done to him and pay him back for his deeds. Personal revenge is ruled out, even when it is dressed up as fairness (compare Romans 12:17).
29.explain:
“Do not say, ‘I will do to him just as he has done to me;’”

The son must not even say it. “I will do to him just as he has done to me.” This is the voice of personal revenge, the desire to pay back exactly what one has received. It feels like fairness, but it is vengeance dressed up as justice.

“I will render to the man according to his work.”

The second line repeats the vow: “I will render to the man according to his work.” In Hebrew the same words describe God’s judgment in 24:12, where He will “render to each man according to his deeds.” Repayment belongs to God, not to the individual. Personal revenge is ruled out, even when it seems fair. Proverbs said earlier, “Do not say, ‘I will recompense evil’; Wait for the LORD, and He will save you” (20:22). Paul says the same: “Repay no one evil for evil” (Romans 12:17).

30.brief: The wise man tells of walking past the field of the lazy man, the vineyard of someone lacking sense. What follows is a lesson drawn from something he saw with his own eyes.
30.explain:
“I went by the field of the lazy man,”

The appendix ends with a story. The wise man tells of walking past “the field of the lazy man.” The lazy man in Proverbs is not someone who cannot work. He is someone who can work and will not. He has a field, which means he has the means of making a living, but he neglects it.

“And by the vineyard of the man devoid of understanding;”

The field is also a “vineyard,” and its owner is “the man devoid of understanding,” in Hebrew literally lacking heart, that is, lacking sense. His problem is not lack of ability but lack of wisdom and self-discipline. What follows is a lesson the wise man drew from something he saw with his own eyes.

31.brief: The field was overgrown with thorns, its ground covered with nettles, and its stone wall broken down. Neglect has done its slow work, and the scene pictures what laziness does to any part of a life left untended.
31.explain:
“And there it was, all overgrown with thorns;”

What the wise man saw was a field “all overgrown with thorns.” Weeds had taken over. Thorns like these do not appear overnight. They spread because no one pulled them.

“Its surface was covered with nettles;”

The ground itself was “covered with nettles,” stinging weeds that made the field useless and painful to walk through. The weeds had crowded the ground that should have been producing a harvest.

“Its stone wall was broken down.”

Worst of all, “Its stone wall was broken down.” The wall protected the vineyard from animals and thieves. With it broken, the field lay open to anyone and anything. The observer names no attacker. What he sees, weeds left unchecked and a wall left in ruins, points to neglect doing its slow work. The scene pictures what laziness does to any part of a life left untended.
31.notes: Stone walls around vineyards kept out animals and intruders. Isaiah’s song of the vineyard pictures judgment as the removal of that protection: “I will take away its hedge, and it shall be burned; And break down its wall” (Isaiah 5:5).

32.brief: Seeing it, he took it to heart and drew a lesson from it. Wisdom learns by careful observation, turning someone else’s ruin into instruction.
32.explain:
“When I saw it, I considered it well;”

The wise man did not just glance at the field and move on. “I considered it well.” He took it to heart, thought about what he saw, and asked what it meant.

“I looked on it and received instruction:”

He “looked on it and received instruction.” He learned from it. Wisdom learns by careful observation, turning someone else’s ruin into a lesson. The fool learns only from his own painful experience, if at all, but the wise man learns from others. He does not say he scolded the lazy man or felt superior to him. He simply let the ruined field teach him, so that his own fields would not end the same way. The lesson he drew follows in 24:33–34.

33.brief: A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest. The lesson he learned repeats 6:10, showing how ruin comes through small, repeated delays that seem harmless.
33.explain:
“A little sleep, a little slumber,”

The observer states his lesson in words that imitate the lazy man’s excuse: “A little sleep, a little slumber.” They are not a conversation he overheard but the kind of thing a lazy person tells himself. Such a person does not plan to ruin his field. He just wants a little more rest. Each delay seems harmless.

“A little folding of the hands to rest;”

“A little folding of the hands to rest.” The folded hands are the picture of idleness. The repetition of “a little” shows how ruin comes: not through one dramatic decision but through small, repeated delays. Each one seems reasonable. Together they leave a field full of thorns. The lesson repeats 6:10 nearly word for word. The danger lies less in one lazy day than in a habit that never notices how much has been lost.
33.notes: Proverbs 6:10–11 has almost the same words; the NKJV ends 6:10 with “to sleep” and 24:33 with “to rest.”

34.brief: Then poverty comes on you like a prowler and need like an armed man. The collection of the words of the wise ends with a sudden, unwelcome visitor as the slow drift of laziness gives way to want (compare 6:11); the warning concerns willful neglect, not poverty that comes from inability or genuine hardship.
34.explain:
“So shall your poverty come like a prowler,”

The end of the lazy man’s little rests is “poverty,” and it comes “like a prowler,” someone who walks about and arrives unexpectedly. The lazy man does not see it coming. One day he wakes to find that want has slipped in.

“And your need like an armed man.”

His “need” comes “like an armed man,” someone he cannot resist or drive away. Poverty arrives suddenly and with force. The collection of the words of the wise ends with this sudden, unwelcome visitor. The slow drift of laziness gives way to want. This repeats 6:11. The warning concerns willful neglect, the choice not to work when one is able. It does not describe poverty that comes from inability, illness, or genuine hardship, and it must never be used to blame the poor.
